name: Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport
before:
Cusco's airport, and the arrival point for Machu Picchu and the wider Cusco Region. It is Peru's second most important air terminal, handling 3,004,412 passengers in 2023, and sits only 3.7 km from the historic centre.

That closeness is also the problem. The airport is hemmed in near the middle of the city and operates at limited capacity as a result. The runway is 3,400 metres, which is long for the traffic, but it needs to be: the thin air at this altitude means aircraft need more room to get airborne.

Ground arrangements are well organised. Authorised taxi firms have counters inside the arrivals hall, and three shuttle operators work the airport, two of them door to door. Sixt, Thrifty, Dollar and Hertz all have offices opposite the main entrance.

One thing to flag. PeruRail sells tickets to Machu Picchu Pueblo and Puno from an office inside the airport, but there is no station at the airport, so a client still needs a taxi or shuttle out to Wanchaq, San Pedro or Poroy to board.

It was the first airport in Peru to use jetways, in May 2000, and is named after Alejandro Velasco Astete, the first pilot to fly across the Andes in 1925.
after:
Cusco's airport, and the arrival point for Machu Picchu and the wider Cusco Region. CORPAC, which runs it, said in June 2026 that it handles about 11,000 passengers a day. It sits only 3.7 km from the historic centre.

That closeness is also the problem. The airport is small and hemmed in near the middle of the city. Its runway is about 3,400 metres long, and the airport is 3,310 metres above sea level.

Shuttle companies work the airport, some with hotel pick-up and drop-off.

One thing to flag. PeruRail sells tickets to Machu Picchu Pueblo and Puno from an office at the airport, but there is no station there, so a client still has to get to Wanchaq, San Pedro or Poroy to board.

It is named after Alejandro Velasco Astete, who made the first flight from Lima to Cusco in 1925.

claims.claim: FCDO: protests can disrupt trains to Machu Picchu; no advice against travel to Cusco
claims.why: Held back, for the record: the FCDO says train services to and from Machu Picchu are occasionally suspended or disrupted by protests, and lists Cusco among regions with recent protests. Its advice against all but essential travel covers the Peru and Colombia border strip and the VRAEM valleys and does not name Cusco or Machu Picchu. Nothing in the old text to replace.

quote: Some train services in the south, including those to and from Machu Picchu, are occasionally suspended or disrupted because of protests.
Other regions that have seen recent protests include Arequipa, Ayacucho, Cusco, La Libertad, Madre de Dios and Puno.

sources.quote: FCDO advises against all but essential travel to the Valley of the Apurímac, Ene, and Mantaro Rivers, also known as the VRAEM region.

claims.claim: runway closures for repairs in 2026
claims.why: Held back, for the record: CORPAC closed the runway until about 10:00 on 14 August 2026 for corrective repairs and told passengers with morning flights to check with their airline; its larger resurfacing programme (announced 30 June 2026) is done at night. One-off events, nothing in the old text to replace.
